title: Pandemics in the age of Twitter: Content analysis of tweets during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak
screen_reason: Manual content analysis of 5,395 randomly sampled H1N1/swine-flu tweets, with an explicit misinformation qualifier coded against CDC / Public Health Agency of Canada and a credible-news-source reference standard. 4.5% of coded tweets were classified as possible misinformation — a share of items in a sample with a stated denominator, i.e. CONTENT.

estimates.country: Not stated (global English-language Twitter; authors note ~50.8% of Twitter users are American)
estimates.date: 9 Mondays four weeks apart between 11 May and 21 December 2009 (archive collected 1 May – 31 December 2009)
estimates.measure_type: % of sampled H1N1/swine-flu tweets manually coded as possible misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 4.5% were classified as possible misinformation (Table 4: Misinform. total 243 (5%) of 5,395; 243/5395 = 4.5%)
estimates.denominator: 5,395 English-language, non-retweet tweets containing 'H1N1', 'swine flu' or 'swineflu', drawn as 25 random tweets per hour on each of 9 sampled days
estimates.definition: Tweet not categorised as a joke and unsubstantiated by the reference standards; may make speculations, express distrust of authority or the media, or include conspiracy or doomsday theories
estimates.misinfo_def: "Tweet contradicts the reference standard or contains unsubstantiated information. May make speculations or express distrust of authority or the media. May include conspiracy or doomsday theories." (Table 2)
estimates.source_quote: common, while 4.5% were classified as possible misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content Analysis' (p. 7); Table 4 'Misinform.' row, Total column
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual coding by the authors using an iteratively developed tri-axial codebook; reference standards were the CDC and the Public Health Agency of Canada for scientific claims and a panel of credible online news sources (e.g. CNN, BBC) for news claims. Inter-rater reliability (kappa) 0.80 for content, 0.74 for qualifiers, 0.84 for links, established on a 125-tweet subset.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweets were categorized as misinformation if the tweet was not categorized as a joke and was unsubstantiated by our reference standards: the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Public Health Agency of Canada for scientific claims and a panel of credible online news sources (e.g., CNN, BBC) for news-related claims.
estimates.notes: Time series collapsed to the pooled total across all 9 sampling days (the paper's own headline figure), as instructed; the per-day range was 2.2–9.2%. Table 4 rounds the same quantity to 5% (243/5,395 = 4.50%); the text's 4.5% is used. IMPORTANT MEASUREMENT CAVEAT: misinformation is a 'qualifier' code, and the methods state 'Tweets not resource or spam-based were coded with a qualifier, if present' — resource tweets (52.6% of the sample, and explicitly 'may or may not be factual') were therefore not eligible for the misinformation label, while the denominator for the 4.5% is all 5,395 tweets. The authors themselves call the estimate conservative (jokes and confusing posts also excluded). Retweets and non-English tweets were excluded from the sample. Definition is broad ('unsubstantiated information', speculation, distrust of authority), hence breadth=misleading.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Per-day misinformation counts in Table 4 (23/600, 13/600, 13/600, 55/600, 37/600, 34/595, 28/600, 26/600, 14/600) and the stated 2.2–9.2% range across time points were not made into rows — time series collapsed to the pooled figure per the protocol. (2) Figure captions give peak-day shares from the AUTOMATED query, not manual coding: Figure 11 'highest peak on Sept. 20 where 1.93% of all tweets expressed misinformation'. Not extracted (single-day automated-query peak, not a representative estimate). Note a probable error in the paper: the Figure 6 caption, which is about humour, also says '9.82% of all tweets expressed misinformation' — apparently a copy-paste slip. (3) Retweet sub-analysis (3 RTs per hour coded) reports no significant difference in misinformation between RTs and non-RTs but gives no misinformation share for RTs, so no separate row. (4) Terminology shift (H1N1 use 8.8% -> 40.5%) and link-source shares (news websites 23.2%, government/public health 1.5%) are not misinformation shares. (5) The automated classifier's misinformation query correlated r = .815 with manual coding but no automated prevalence figure is given for the corpus.

rob.design: Infoveillance study. Over 2 million tweets archived 1 May – 31 December 2009 via the Twitter API using the keywords 'H1N1', 'swine flu', 'swineflu'. For manual coding, 25 tweets were randomly selected from every hour of 9 Mondays four weeks apart (600/day; 595 on 28 September) = 5,395; retweets and non-English tweets excluded. No formal sample size calculation ('no prior methodologies for sampling tweets'). Codebook developed iteratively from 1,200 pilot tweets; two raters coded a 125-tweet subset to establish reliability; kappa 0.80 (content), 0.74 (qualifiers), 0.84 (links). Authors flag the lack of a well-defined study population, no geocoding, and unknown user demographics as the principal limitations.
rob.item6_quote: Tweets were categorized as misinformation if the tweet was not categorized as a joke and was unsubstantiated by our reference standards: the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Public Health Agency of Canada for scientific claims and a panel of credible online news sources (e.g., CNN, BBC) for news-related claims.
rob.item10_quote: However, we classified only 4.5% of manually coded tweets as possible misinformation or speculation. Although this amount ranged from 2.2 to 9.2% across our 9 time points, increasing amounts of misinformation did not occur until August, months after initial media reports.
